claims.text: In Q235 steel, corrosion-related degradation versus protection in aggressive high-temperature salt environments is primarily controlled by the integrity and adherence of the surface iron-oxide film.
A continuous, adherent oxide scale limits inward diffusion of corrosive species and preserves the Q235 substrate.
A discontinuous or spalled oxide layer accelerates degradation of Q235 steel.
As-received Q235 steel typically has a ferrite-pearlite microstructure and low alloying content.
Controlled annealing in an oxygen-containing atmosphere can produce a uniform, adherent iron-oxide film on Q235 steel.
Molten FLiBe exposure at about 700 °C is a relevant aggressive high-temperature corrosion condition.
Oxide-formation kinetics are minimal at room temperature relative to approximately 700 °C.
The intervention improves corrosion resistance only when temperature and oxygen partial pressure permit formation of a continuous protective oxide film.
Oxide-scale continuity, thickness, and adhesion, together with underlying grain-boundary characteristics, mediate Q235 corrosion behavior.
The protective oxide film on Q235 is expected to consist primarily of Fe3O4 and/or Fe2O3.
A continuous iron-oxide film acts as a physical and kinetic barrier to aggressive fluoride ingress in molten salt.
Rapid grain-boundary diffusion, discontinuous oxide formation, or oxide spallation causes localized dissolution and accelerated mass loss.
Pre-treated Q235 samples bearing a well-adherent oxide layer will exhibit lower mass loss than untreated samples after high-temperature salt exposure.
Pre-treated Q235 samples bearing a well-adherent oxide layer will exhibit less microstructural degradation and shallower corrosion than untreated samples.
Differences between pre-treated and untreated Q235 samples will be much less pronounced at room temperature.
Strongly reducing conditions that hinder oxide formation should suppress the proposed protective mechanism.
Rapid thermal cycling that causes oxide spallation should suppress the proposed protective mechanism.
Protective oxide-film behavior is well established in higher-alloy steels.
The cited FLiBe study demonstrates substantial, alloy-dependent mass loss and selective elemental dissolution at 700 °C.
